title: Running big games on small handhelds

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What if your Nintendo Switch could show your gaming PC's screen, with a live panel showing exactly how the stream is doing?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like a fun weekend project. Is that real?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is. Antoine maintains three homebrew repos with one shared itch: run something interesting on hardware that wasn't designed for it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Artemis-Switch is his fork of Moonlight-Switch, tuned for Apollo hosts, which are the Sunshine family of streaming servers. He streams Steam Big Picture from his desktop and plays on the Switch, which just acts as a screen.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What's in the app that makes it special?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: An overlay with two tabs. Quick holds window shortcuts, keyboard presets and Apollo host scripts, so you can manage the PC without leaving the stream. Performance shows bitrate, around twelve megabits in the screenshot, Wi-Fi bars, and receive, decode and render timings.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And those timings tell a story.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: They do. Receive and decode come in under a millisecond, which means the network and decoder are comfortable, and the frame budget goes mostly to drawing the picture.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: moonlight-N3DS brings a GameStream client to the New 3DS, with its small top screen and software decoding. The win is simply having a Moonlight path on a 2015 handheld. And sm64coopdx-switch is a Switch port of the cooperative Super Mario 64 project, with online co-op and Lua mods. You supply your own game copy; the repo holds the port source.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. Artemis-Switch streams a PC, the 3DS client streams on older hardware, and the Mario port runs natively. The written page has a comparison table and screenshots of the overlay.
